There are many benefits to managing your anger well. However, there are pitfalls along that path, and being aware of them can help you to be fruitful as you try to keep your anger in check.

Anger management strategies can fail or fall short when they are only skin deep. There is a strategy where you count slowly down from ten, and it’s a way to help you slow down before you respond rashly. This strategy does work in the moment, but it’s important to address the underlying heart issues. Anger can resurface and become harder to control.

Sticking with anger management strategies can also be difficult if you’re relying solely on willpower. For sustained and lasting change, we need the Lord’s help as well as accountability from others. The encouragement and support we get from other people can help us stay on the path, and the work of the Spirit in us can bring about true transformation in our hearts.

In other circumstances, anger management strategies don’t stick because we ignore the root causes of anger. Anger may be a momentary response, but many other things, such as learned patterns of behavior, often inform it. Other underlying causes of anger could be stress, unforgiveness, or unresolved trauma, which can fuel your anger and unhealthy responses to situations.

Awareness of these potential pitfalls can help you make good use of anger management strategies that help you keep anger in check. At the same time, you can address the deeper issues that could be informing your anger.

Effective Anger Management Strategies to Help You Control Anger

There are many strategies that you can use to help you manage your anger. It’s important to remember that anger management isn’t about suppressing your anger or pretending it doesn’t exist. Those are different ways of handling anger poorly. Rather, the goal is to develop a healthy relationship with your anger, to be able to understand your own anger, and channel it constructively instead of letting it take the reins.

Some effective anger management strategies include the following:

Pause, and pray: Allow yourself to count down from ten, or to leave the room briefly when you can, to allow yourself space to calm down. Stepping out of the situation can make a difference. When you feel anger rising, pause, breathe, and pray. Ask the Lord to help you stay calm and respond wisely, instead of being guided by your emotions.

Identify your triggers: Your anger works in ways that are unique to you. Reflect on the situations that tend to make your anger flare up. Recognize your own patterns of anger, like when you’re tired, hungry, stressed, or feeling vulnerable. Knowing these patterns helps you to anticipate your anger and manage it before it flares up or escalates.

Reframe your thoughts: Often, anger can be magnified because of our thinking patterns. If someone makes a hurtful joke or comment, it might not necessarily be intentional. Assuming it is can cause anger to flare up. It’s better to presume otherwise until you have further information. Meditating on Scripture about patience and self-control can also help to reshape your responses to triggering situations.

Use healthy outlets: Anger ought to be expressed, and there are healthy ways to do this. Using art or other forms of creative expression like writing, exercise and other physical activity, or talking things out with a trusted confidante can help you to release the tension of anger without damaging yourself or other people.

Practice forgiveness: Grudges and resentment can harbor and nurture anger. Instead, choose to forgive, releasing yourself from the burden of resentment or the need to get even.

Develop communication and problem-solving skills: There are times when you feel angry because you feel helpless or can’t express your concerns clearly. When you can plan and act to overcome challenges, and when you can work through issues amicably, it can prevent frustrations from taking over.

Seek help: Anger management therapy can help you dig deep to understand the underlying causes of your anger. You can also learn how to reframe your thoughts and implement strategies to help keep your anger under control. Help isn’t far from you; reach out to our office to connect with an anger management counselor today.

Uncontrolled anger can wreak havoc in your life by stirring up conflict, leading you to utter hurtful words you otherwise wouldn’t, or taking you down the path to actions you later regret.

There is a Proverb that says, “An angry person stirs up conflict, and a hot-tempered person commits many sins.” (Proverbs 29:22, NIV) If anger begins controlling you, it becomes a chronic problem. Such anger has spiritual consequences, such as derailing your walk with the Lord (James 1:19-22). Chronic anger can also increase your stress levels and negatively impact your physical health by increasing your blood pressure and the risk of heart disease.

Anger can also build walls between people, especially when that anger makes them feel unsafe around you. Anger, then, can be quite devastating.

The above probably gives anger a bad rap by pointing out all of the negative impacts of anger. Remember, anger isn’t sinful in itself. Responding appropriately to those cues helps you communicate your needs effectively with others. This can mean fostering deeper trust and intimacy when you give gentle responses to tense situations.

Being in control of your anger and managing it well can also mean better health as you lower your stress levels, open yourself up more to the Lord’s peace, and yield more and more to the Spirit’s guidance. item.title: How to Improve Communication in a Relationship in a Digital World
item.description:
Communication is important in every aspect of life. It’s so important that entire college degrees are centered on communication. Psychologists work carefully with clients to help them learn how to be more effective communicators, and multi-million dollar business deals rely on it. The world of art centers on conveying ideas through visual presentation.

Even the Bible talks about communication and how it affects our lives. It talks about the importance of speaking the truth and helping to build each other up (Ephesians 4:15, Ephesians 4:29). It tells us to be quick to listen and describes the fallout when we don’t (James 1:19, Proverbs 27:6).

It’s clear that communicating ideas effectively is important for nearly every facet of life, but it’s particularly important in relationships. Even if your communication isn’t the best, you can learn how to improve communication in a relationship.

Shouldn’t Communication Be Improving?

One would think that with all the connectivity that our modern age affords us, communication would be improving. Unfortunately, that is simply not true. Modern conveniences like texting and email may provide us with instant access to the people in our lives, but it doesn’t guarantee quality communication.

Texting

Much of our modern conversations happen through texting. While texting allows people to stay in touch more easily, it also undermines the authentic beauty of face-to-face communication. And texting can often cause a lack of clarity in content and intent.

The nuances of in-person conversations, the flicker of the eyes, micro-facial expressions, and voice inflections are all gone when communication is reduced to words on a screen. Even though the use of emojis can give more clarity and context than words alone, there is still a discrepancy between the effectiveness of in-person communication and what is done over text.

Out of Practice

Not only does this texting deteriorate the quality of communication, but it can also affect your ability to communicate in general. Just like all other skills, communication is a learned skill that needs to be practiced to be perfected. When texting and other digital means become the main source of communication, your ability to interact in person can suffer.

Avoidance

Most people will avoid conflict when they can, and the internet affords you that luxury. It’s often easier to avoid difficult conversations by leaving people “on read” or ghosting them entirely than it is to have a conflict. Because the internet allows physical distance in communication, it enables you to avoid conversations that really should take place.

Misunderstandings

Many conflicts and misunderstandings, even broken relationships, could be avoided if people were simply willing to say what they actually mean and actively listen to one another. Misunderstandings abound online where tone and intent are easily misread. Without the benefit of facial expressions, body language, and even voice inflections, it’s tempting for your audience to fill in the gap in communication with their own assumptions.

How to Improve Communication

The good news is that communication is a skill. Like any other skill, it can be improved with practice and intentional effort, even in the digital age.

Be Quick to Listen

Scripture says to be “quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry” (James 1:19, NIV). When you actively listen, you’re allowing the person you’re talking with to feel heard, and that builds trust. To do this in a practical sense, you should prioritize in-person conversations over digital communication and put away your device when you do. This helps you give your full attention to the person in front of you.

If you’re communicating digitally, you can still be an active listener by fully reading text or comments rather than skimming for important information and perhaps missing important details in the process.

Speak Clearly

Saying what you mean in a kind and respectful, even direct way helps to eliminate confusion and reduces the chance of hurt feelings. Avoid vague or passive language and get into the habit of using concise words to express your thoughts in a way that leaves no room for confusion.

Be Honest

While it seems like speaking honestly should go without saying, a lack of authenticity can deteriorate friendships and shut communication down. Ephesians 4 encourages believers to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15, NIV). While honesty is the expectation in communication, it should also be tempered with love.

Being honest also requires you to be vulnerable. Digital communication can act as a shield sometimes. It allows you to curate a version of yourself that is filtered and edited, void of authenticity. Later in the fourth chapter of Ephesians, we’re told to “put off falsehood” (Ephesians 4:25, NIV). In this context, it shows that we must be willing to share ourselves with others in an unedited, unfiltered state.

Address Issues Directly

Matthew 18:15 shows the importance of going directly to someone when there’s a problem instead of allowing anger and resentment to fester or manifest in a less healthy way. This is a good practice in the modern world, too.

Don’t allow issues to grow or involve other people unnecessarily. In the digital world, it can be tempting to ignore issues or to vent online. But part of being honest is also going directly to the person you have an issue with, rather than allowing that issue to be aired online in a public forum or ignoring the issue altogether.

Practice Patience

If you’re a Christ-follower, you know all about grace and patience. God extended it to you when you accepted Christ, and He continues to forgive, over and over again. The Bible calls us to do the same: “Bear with each other and forgive one another.” (Colossians 3:13, NIV) You will inevitably have misunderstandings and bad communication days. But you can consciously choose patience instead of reactionary behavior to help mitigate the negative effects.

Make Echoing a Habit

Implement active verification into your communication to ward off misunderstandings. In person, you probably do this naturally with a nod of your head or the occasional “uh-huh.” But online, you have to do it manually.

Before you react to a text that feels potentially hurtful, ask for clarification. Ask something like, “Am I understanding correctly that you…” Not only does this demand clarification, but this small pivot in the conversation helps you to practice being slow to anger.

Don’t Blame Technology Entirely

While it’s easy to blame modern communication problems on the internet, the truth is that, while online communication does have its limitations, it’s not entirely to blame. Technology doesn’t create communication flaws; it just amplifies them.

A smartphone doesn’t make you a reactionary person. It just gives you the tools to act on your reactions and may amplify the effect. If you struggle with honesty, the internet may give you a convenient and easy platform on which to deceive. Consider how you use technology and why. This will help clarify what lies beneath your digital communications.

Adhere to the Two Text Rule

Some conversations are just too complicated or important to take place over text. A rule to follow for relationships is that if a disagreement or a complex topic isn’t resolved in two text exchanges, the conversation should be moved immediately to a voice call or in person conversation. This prevents assumptions from being made.

Therapy Can Help You Improve Communication in Your Relationships

If you need help learning how to be a better communicator, make an appointment with one of our Christian therapists today. Sometimes an outside perspective can make it easier to recognize patterns in your own life, which can help you find healthier ways to express your emotions and thoughts. In therapy, you can also learn how to be a better listener and how to overcome any habits that might be interfering with your communication.

Digital communication is faster, but not necessarily better. Technology may shape how you communicate, but it doesn’t change the importance of listening well, speaking the truth, and treating others with kindness. Words matter, even if they are just on a screen.

Connect with this office for a risk-free consultation to see how Christian therapy can help you improve your communication.

item.title: The Purpose of Mindfulness in Counseling
item.description:
In the world of counseling psychology and therapy, the concept of mindfulness has been growing in both popularity and interest over the last several decades. As this trend has grown, researchers have brought additional evidence to support the use of mindfulness practices in counseling and therapy sessions.

In this article, I’d like to bring attention to the effectiveness of mindfulness, some of the clinical evidence that supports its use, as well as some practical techniques, trauma-informed applications, and how we can integrate mindfulness practices into our Christian spiritual formation.

Before we dive into some of the particularities of mindfulness, let’s first answer the question, “What is mindfulness?”

Mindfulness is a practice that asks the participant to deliberately and intentionally focus his/her attention on their present experience in a nonjudgmental way. Furthermore, mindfulness is a state that helps individuals become more aware of physical, mental, and emotional conditions without judgment. In other words, it can be described as a state of focused attention, paying particular attention to the moment, in a nonjudgmental way.

Clinical Evidence for the Use of Mindfulness Techniques

Research done through the American Counseling Association found that mindfulness is used in the treatment of a variety of mental-health concerns such as intellectual disorders, autism spectrum, trauma, eating disorders, anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, and sexual dysfunction disorders. Additionally, mindfulness techniques can be paired with different therapeutic modalities to enhance the healing process and spur on deeper transformation.

An article published by Positive Psychology states that mindfulness (through mindfulness-based interventions) changes neural pathways in the brain related to rumination, worry, self-regulation, compassion, attention, emotional reactivity, and affect.

Put more simply, clinical evidence shows that the practice of mindfulness helps change your brain’s thinking patterns. Furthermore, it changes the structure of your brain’s neural pathways, which ultimately allows you to change what you think about and how you think.

In my own work with clients, mindfulness practices have started to become a regular part of my practice. By facilitating a moment to pause and bring attention to the moment by noticing breathing patterns, what sensations are occurring in the body, and what emotions are present, clients commonly express experiencing a greater depth of calm.

This is because mindfulness techniques and practices not only impact the brain, but also the sympathetic and parasympathetic branches of the nervous system. These intricate internal systems are also responsible for connecting to deeper sensations of relaxation and stress relief.

Practical Ways That Mindfulness Can Be Used

Some of the most common mindfulness practices and techniques involve your attention and your breath. Since we live in such a fast-paced world, it can be easy to lose sight of the moment. Our minds are constantly thinking about “the next thing.” Or we’re scrolling on our phones, responding to texts, emails, or social media posts. With our attention consistently being drawn elsewhere, mindfulness seeks to slow us down (in a positive way).

Our breath is an easy access point or signal to our internal states, or what’s happening inside of us. Our breath is also always with us (thank God) and isn’t something we have to dig for. By beginning to focus attention on the breath, the mind can begin to settle, not rushing from one thing to another. Your breath is present with you. Your body is present with you. God is present with you.

As mentioned earlier, focused and nonjudgmental attention are two major tenets in mindfulness practices. We are often our harshest critics. When the inner critic becomes too loud, mindfulness can help you reset your thoughts and feelings to help you not get stuck in your head. Here is a basic outline you can use:

Breath Take one minute and focus on your breathing pattern. What characteristics do you notice? Is your breathing shallow or is it deep? Don’t try to change your breathing; just notice it.

Action Ask yourself the question, “Is there a particular action that my body is wanting to do right now?” As you sit with your breath and this question, notice what comes to mind.

Sensation Continuing to breathe, ask yourself, “What sensations am I experiencing in my body right now?” Take a minute to notice these sensations and where you feel them.

Emotion Continuing to breathe, take one more minute to notice what emotions you’re feeling on the inside. Joy? Frustration? Sadness? Again, you shouldn’t be judging what you’re feeling, simply noticing.

An exercise like this can be done in about 4-5 minutes, get you in touch with your body and your nervous system, and promote a deeper sense of regulation.

Trauma-Informed Applications of Mindfulness Practices

For someone who has experienced trauma, one of the most important things in recovery is helping the person to be grounded in the moment. Traumatic events commonly cause someone to flee from the moment.

This is because their body (aka their nervous system) had a sense that being present in the specific trauma would have been too painful for them to bear. However, when the person is no longer in that specific traumatic moment, their nervous system may still be holding onto the belief that anywhere is safer than the moment.

This is why mindfulness practices can be so incredibly effective and helpful in trauma recovery. By practicing mindfulness – a state of focused attention, paying particular attention to the moment, in a nonjudgmental way – the person is essentially retraining their own nervous system to trust that the moment is safe.

The purpose of helping those who have experienced trauma be grounded in the moment is to anchor them back into reality. When a person is legitimately triggered, their brain and nervous system cannot tell the difference between the present and the past.

Often the person begins to act, feel, and think as if they’re actually back in the traumatic situation. As they become flooded with distress, their nervous system begins to kick into overdrive, propelling them to try anything and everything to get back to a place of safety both emotionally and physically.

Using mindfulness practices in this instance helps the person orient themselves to the reality they’re actually in. Some of these include the 5-4-3-2-1 Method, which invites the person to look around them and name five things they can see, four they can touch, etc. Another includes a breathing method like the 4-7-8 technique. Each exercise is designed to ground the person in the present and reduce distress in the nervous system.

How does mindfulness integrate with faith in God?

There are many contemplative Christian spiritual practices that can be intertwined with using mindfulness in counseling and throughout the day. The majority of these practices revolve around prayer. Two examples of this are what is known as Listening Prayer and Meditative Prayer (Christian Meditation).

It is important to note here that secular mindfulness practice often focuses on emptying the mind in order to find or attain peace. Christian meditative practices, however, focus on stilling oneself in the presence of God to be filled with His presence and listen for His voice. The goal of each is the same: hear God’s voice and be filled by Him.

Listening Prayer is exactly what it sounds like: a posture of prayer where someone is listening for God’s voice. Jamie and Donna Winship are an excellent resource if you’re interested in learning more about this practice. Here is a simple four-step model you can use to start out or grow in this practice:

Be still Quiet yourself in the presence of God.

Be looking Look for a vision or pictures in your mind as you pray and seek God.

Be listening God’s voice often comes as the free flow of thoughts that light upon your mind as you’re focusing your attention on Jesus.

Be writing Write out the free flow of thoughts, pictures, images that come as you’re focusing on Jesus.

Again, the emphasis here is that attention is being focused on Jesus. This is not an exercise to empty the mind, but rather to shift focused attention and train our hearts and minds to seek Jesus.

Christian Meditation is another prayer model used with the goal of quieting ourselves in God’s presence to hear from Him and be filled by Him. This is ultimately to grow closer to God. Hallow is an app that helps people walk through the practice of Christian Meditation. Here are some of the steps they have outlined:

Find a comfortable place to pray God meets us where we are – it doesn’t have to be perfect. Just make sure you feel like you can be yourself with God in this place, whether you’re alone or in public.

Prepare your heart and mind for prayer Think about your prayer before starting to pray. Is there anything on my mind that I want to offer to God in prayer? Are there things preventing me from resting with God?

Select a prayer, verse, or word to meditate on In Christian meditation, we always meditate on something holy that will fill our hearts and bring us closer to God.

Let God fill your heart Remember: it’s not as much about what we say in prayer but how well we prepare ourselves to listen to God’s voice in the silence.

End with thanksgiving and gratitude Conclude your time in prayer by thanking God for this time with you.

As we come to the end, I hope that you’re leaving with a better understanding of the usefulness of practicing mindfulness and how it can be applied in various aspects of your life. As a counselor, these are tools I enjoy integrating into my work with clients.

If reading this article sparked your interest or curiosity, I would love to hear from you! I am currently taking on new clients in both Green Lake and Bothell locations, as well as online throughout Washington State.

item.title: What Are the Different Attachment Types and Why Do They Matter?
item.description:
Attachment Theory

In this modern age of pop psychology, many people are starting to hear about attachment theory. Some may even be able to tell you their exact attachment style. If you’re new to the idea of attachment theory, you may be curious about exactly what it is and what purpose it serves.

John Bowlby, a psychologist from the mid-twentieth century, founded the idea of Attachment Theory. In the 1950s, he described attachment behavior as behavior whereby an individual attains or maintains a connection to another clearly identified individual seen as better able to cope with the world (Bowlby, 1982).

Another psychologist, Mary Ainsworth, later tested his theory of connection with infants ranging from 9-30 months in age to see how they would react to short periods of separation from their caregivers (Ainsworth, 1978). Her findings, and the findings of later studies, informed the types of attachment styles and how these styles impact both children and adults.

Types of Attachment Style

“Attachment styles comprise cognitions relating to both the self (‘Am I worthy of love’) and others (‘Can I depend on others during times of stress’)” (Huang, 2026). Attachments begin in infancy. God designed us this way.

Consider the beginning of Scripture where God says, “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him.” (Gen. 2:18, ESV BibleGateway.com). God’s original plan was to have a right relationship with Him and with others, just as He is in relationship with Himself as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Unfortunately, due to sin entering the world, our relationships with others are not perfect. Because of this, while secure attachments do exist, there are three types of attachment styles that are insecure: anxious-preoccupied, dismissive-avoidant, and disorganized, otherwise known as fearful-avoidant. The following excerpt from Simply Psychology has a breakdown of each:

Secure Attachment: Securely attached individuals are comfortable with intimacy and can balance dependence and independence in relationships.

Preoccupied Attachment (Anxious in Children): Individuals with this attachment style crave intimacy and can be overly dependent and demanding in relationships.

Dismissive Attachment (Avoidant in Children): This style is characterized by a strong sense of self-sufficiency, often to the point of appearing detached. Individuals with dismissive attachment value their independence highly and may seem uninterested in close relationships.

Fearful Attachment (Disorganized in Children): Individuals with a fearful attachment style desire close relationships and fear vulnerability. They may behave unpredictably in relationships due to their internal conflict between a desire for intimacy and fear of it (Huang, 2026).

A further breakdown of the behaviors that help identify each attachment style is as follows:

Secure

  • Healthy communication and management of conflict
  • Healthy view of self, others, and God
  • Regulated emotions
  • Ability to trust and connect with self, others, and God
  • Feeling comfortable alone
  • Being emotionally available for others

Anxious-Preoccupied

  • Feeling unworthy of connection
  • Highly sensitive to criticism
  • Uncomfortable with being alone
  • Low self-esteem
  • Difficulty with trusting self, others, or God
  • Feelings of jealousy
  • Fearing rejection or abandonment

Dismissive-Avoidant

  • Strong sense of independence
  • Easily dismiss others
  • Difficulty with trusting others or God
  • Avoiding emotional or physical intimacy
  • Having issues with commitment

Fearful-Avoidant

  • Having difficulty trusting self, others, and God
  • Struggling to regulate emotions
  • Showing signs of both anxious and avoidant attachment styles
  • Fearing rejection
  • Showing signs of confusing and contradictory behaviors (Cleveland Clinic, 2026).

Examples of Each Attachment in the Bible

Forming attachments is an unavoidable part of the human experience. Whether we have a secure or insecure attachment, the type we possess has wide-ranging consequences for how we view ourselves, others, and even how we view God. The following biblical figures map these styles with startling accuracy:

Secure

Ruth, who followed Naomi after the death of her husband and entrusted herself to Naomi and to God.

“Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” – Ruth 1:16, ESV

John, the beloved disciple of Jesus, to whom Jesus entrusted his mother.

When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, ‘Woman, behold your son!’ Then he said to the disciple, ‘Behold your mother!’ And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. – John 19:26-27, ESV

Anxious-Preoccupied

King David, who openly expresses throughout the Psalms his fear and anxiety of being abandoned by God.

“O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath! For your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me…O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you. My heart throbs; my strength fails me, and the light of my eyes – it also has gone from me…Do not forsake me, O Lord! O my God, be not far from me! Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation!” – Psalm 38:1-2, 9-10, 21-22, ESV

Dismissive-Avoidant

Jonah, who, at God’s call to witness to the Ninevites, fled the complete opposite direction.

Now the word of the Lord came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, ‘Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.’ But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord. – Jonah 1:1-3, ESV

Fearful-Avoidant

The nation of Israel after God saved them from the Egyptians, led them with pillars of cloud and fire, gave them water in the desert, and fed them manna from heaven.

Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off and said to Moses, ‘You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die.’ – Exodus 20:18-19, ESV

While these are exemplary models of specific attachments, I do not mean to suggest that these people can be universally typed according to Attachment Theory. Rather, these examples model known attachment behaviors and are thus useful for informing this article.

What is Earned Secure Attachment?

If you have read through and identified with any of the insecure attachment behaviors, the good news is that your attachment is not set in stone. Whether you had a difficult childhood that has led to trust issues, fear, and anxiety, or whether adult relationships have damaged your sense of self and trust in God and others, healing is possible.

Through therapy, forming healthy relationships, prayer, and practicing gentle self-reflection, you can build an earned secure attachment style.

But what exactly does “earned secure” mean, and what does it look like? A person with an earned secure attachment has “achieved a secure relationship with their own story. They can discuss their past clearly, acknowledge its impact on them, and hold their early caregivers with a mixture of realism and compassion – without being overwhelmed by grief, dismissive of the experience, or incoherent when describing it. (Simply Psychology, 2026).

EMDR, Lifespan Integration, Internal Family Systems (IFS), or other attachment-based therapies have proven effective in healing attachment wounds and moving clients toward forming stronger, healthier relationships with self, God, and others.

If you’ve found this article helpful in identifying an insecure attachment in yourself, it is never too late to take the first steps toward transforming how you view yourself, others, and even how you view God. God wants you to live life to the full. Therapy can help you get started.

References:
Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., & Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of attachment: A psychological study of the strange situation. Hillsdale, NJ: Erlbaum.
Bowlby, J. (1982). Attachment and loss: Retrospect and prospect. American Journal of Orthopsychiatry, 52(4), 664–678. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1939-0025.1982.tb01456.x
Huang, S. (2026, April 20). Attachment styles in relationships. Simply Psychology. https://www.simplypsychology.org/attachment-styles.html
Professional, C. C. M. (2026, February 13). Attachment styles. Cleveland Clinic. https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/25170-attachment-styles
Simply Psychology. (2026, May 15). Earned Secure attachment: How adults can develop a secure attachment style. https://www.simplypsychology.com/articles/earned-secure- attachment

Photos:
“Lock”, Courtesy of My Foto Canva, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Locks”, Courtesy of alexander ehrenhöfer, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post What Are the Different Attachment Types and Why Do They Matter? appeared first on Spokane Christian Counseling.

item.title: Good Mental Health and the Role of Truth
item.description:
If you spend a significant portion of your time around Generation Alpha, you will invariably hear the phrase “touch grass.” My understanding of this phrase is that it is used by Generation Alpha to encourage a person who spends much of their time online to reconnect with something real, such as grass. It is a simple phrase, but it has a rather deep philosophical truth at its root.

Good Mental Health and Contact with Reality

The philosophical truth at the root is that something begins to go wrong with a person when they have not had regular contact with reality. Reality in its traditional sense, means those parts of our world that we perceive with our senses and interact with through our senses. I agree with this philosophical truth and would also contend that maintaining good mental health requires maintaining contact with reality.

We currently live in a world where there are so many sources of information and so much access to various belief systems that reality can be difficult to decipher. It has become a generally accepted fact in our society that the more time one spends consuming social media and online content, the more symptoms of mental health disorders are experienced. In other words, more time spent consuming social media and online content leads to a decrease in mental health.

Our minds were not made to consume this much information at such a rapid rate. We do not have the capacity to distinguish between what is reality and what is not reality when we consume information at such rapid rates and from so many different sources. It becomes increasingly difficult to maintain contact with reality and to maintain good mental health.

One reason why this rapid and overwhelming consumption of information brings a decline in mental health is that it involves the health of our minds. One of the main purposes of our mind is to recognize reality in order to determine truth. Truth can be defined as beliefs based on reality. I will state that again: mental health involves the health of our minds, and one of the main purposes of our mind is to recognize reality in order to determine truth.

When the purpose for which our minds are made becomes difficult to achieve, the health of our mind declines. There tends to be a lot of overlap when we are discussing our mind and our brains. To be clear, when I use the term “mind,” I am referring to an immaterial part of us.

To put it in traditional Christian philosophical terms, we generally separate the mind into two main parts: the intellect and the will. The purpose of the intellect is to know what is true and good, and the purpose of the will is to make decisions and act on the known truth and the known good. If we cannot determine the truth and what is good, then the health of our mind declines, as it is not able to function properly.

Reality and Truth

This can go both ways. The difficulty with determining reality and truth can lead to mental health disorder symptoms, and mental health disorder symptoms can make it difficult to determine reality and truth. While determining the cause is essential, whatever the cause is, reconnecting with reality can help alleviate symptoms and improve mental health.

For example, one of the key characteristics of someone who suffers from anxiety is that there is an overestimation of the danger of a perceived threat. Perhaps it is anxiety over social interactions with peers. The anxiety might look like a child believing that if the interaction doesn’t go well, everyone in the entire school will make fun of them for the rest of their lives.

Whatever the cause of this anxious thought is, it is helpful to connect with the reality and truth of the likelihood of this perceived outcome. The truth is that, in all likelihood, even if some peers make fun of the child, not all will, and the probability of everyone making fun of the child for the rest of their lives is slim. Presenting this truth to an anxious person can be helpful and allow the person to challenge the anxious thought and ultimately decrease the intensity of the anxiety.

This is just one example of one symptom of one mental health disorder that can be decreased in intensity through reconnecting with reality and truth. I would contend that the same is true for any mental health disorder; reconnecting with reality and truth can decrease symptoms and increase mental health. This becomes important when one is choosing who to listen to or who to seek guidance from regarding mental health.

The Reality of Absolute Truth

Many people do not believe that there is such a thing as truth. They might be more open to the idea of reality, but some believe that even this too is subjective. If connection to reality and truth can increase mental health and disconnecting from reality and truth decreases mental health, it is vital to understand the philosophy that one adheres to before taking advice or guidance from them regarding mental health.

It is important to note that reconnecting with reality and truth can decrease the intensity of symptoms over time, though not always immediately. Often, acknowledging reality and truth can raise the intensity of symptoms for a time. For example, when someone has experienced a loss, it is typical for denial to set in. As an attempt to protect oneself from emotional pain, one may deny the reality of the loss.

However, it is essential that eventually, one acknowledges the loss. Imagine someone losing their job. There is time for denial, but if one were not to acknowledge the reality of the job loss, all sorts of unhelpful consequences would follow. Unhelpful consequences include showing up to a job where you are no longer employed, not looking for another source of income, or not having income and not being able to pay bills.

In this example, acknowledging the loss of a job is emotionally painful, stressful, and likely to produce anxiety. These sufferings are temporary but not acknowledging it bears long-lasting consequences that will bring long-lasting emotional pain, stress, and anxiety.

Reality and truth matter to Christians, because reality and truth matter to God. Scripture tells us that God purposefully and lovingly created all things, visible and invisible, and all these things have purpose. God told His people who He was and who He was not. Jesus taught us what is good and what is not. He taught us what is true and what is not true.

The serpent’s first move in Scripture was to call into question reality and the truth about God. In the garden, the serpent said, “Did God really tell you that?” Then the serpent said that what God had told Adam and Eve was not true. If you’ve read the Bible, you know what happened next. From the beginning of time, reality and truth were what the life of humanity hinged upon. Failing to acknowledge both can cause our relationships to rupture and suffer.

Good mental health and emotional pain are not incompatible

Connecting with and acknowledging reality and truth can sometimes be painful and can even cause suffering. But to live disconnected from reality and truth is even more painful and causes even more suffering. The difficult and sometimes confusing fact about good mental health is that one can be in good mental health and still suffer immense emotional pain.

Due to the fallen world that we live in, reality and truth can be quite painful at times. It is a common and understandable error in thought that the goal of mental health counseling is to help one to feel comfortable and happy in life. Sometimes, over time, a person does feel more comfortable and happier in life by achieving good mental health, but that would be a byproduct of being more connected with reality and truth, not an end goal.

The health of our minds has to do with how grounded we are in reality and truth, not about how we may happen to feel at any given moment. If the ultimate truth is that we were created by an all-loving Creator who made us on purpose and for a purpose, and that we are always loved by Him, then our ability to stay connected to this truth would bring us peace and joy, well beyond the fleeting feelings of comfort and happiness.

Peace and joy can be experienced at the same time as suffering and at the same time as unhappiness and discomfort.

In conclusion, to achieve good mental health, it is essential to connect with reality and truth. Our minds were created for reality and truth. We were created to connect to the world and others through our senses, and to recognize and submit to God’s truth with our minds.

Just as painful and difficult procedures and practices are often necessary for physical health, so too it is often necessary to go through pain and difficulty to improve one’s mental health. Some truths and realities are too difficult to face alone.

Christian Counseling for Good Mental Health

In these scenarios, it can be helpful and beneficial to seek support and guidance from a mental health counselor. Although this does not take away the pain and suffering, the intensity of the pain and suffering can be eased by walking through it with another person to guide you.

“Grasslands”, Courtesy of Neil Mark Thomas, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post Good Mental Health and the Role of Truth appeared first on Seattle Christian Counseling.

item.title: How to Soothe the Fight, Flight, Freeze, and Fawn Response
item.description:
Fight, flight, freeze, and fawn are commonly known as stress responses. The nervous system activates this response to protect you from danger. Unfortunately, due to daily stressors, our minds and bodies now assume danger in anything that causes worry or stress. We no longer fear apex predators; we are anxious about mortgages or rent, utilities, car payments, medical bills, student loans, work, and relationships.

The body responds to these stimuli by activating the sympathetic nervous system, eliciting one or more of these responses.

Understanding the responses

Understanding the responses can lead to better managing the experience when activated. While the fight, flight, and freeze responses have been known for some time, the fawn response is newer and comes from the study of nervous system responses.

Each response is the body’s way of trying to protect itself and presents differently for everyone. However, each response has common experiences. The fight response does not always mean fight in a physical sense. It can look like being irritable, defensive, feeling anger, and/or aggression.

The flight response can look like avoiding, panicking, chronic worry, and/or wanting to run away or flee. The freeze response can look like depression, feeling stuck, dissociation, feeling like your mind “goes blank,” feeling confused, and/or being passive. The fawn response can look like avoiding conflict, people-pleasing (or codependency), and/or difficulty with setting healthy boundaries.

All of these responses are not necessarily unhealthy. Most of them can be helpful when the situation requires it. When there is continuous or constant activation, it can lead to unhelpful or unhealthy experiences.

Why the Sympathetic Nervous System Cannot Stay Stuck in Overdrive

The sympathetic nervous system can get stuck due to chronic stress or severe trauma. When the stress response kicks into overdrive, you can experience physical, emotional, and mental issues.

Chronic stress can cause the following symptoms and conditions (and is not exhaustive):

  • Chronic high blood pressure
  • Increased risk of heart disease
  • Rapid heart rate or palpitations
  • Tension headaches
  • Unexplained aches and pains
  • Digestive problems, like Irritable Bowel Syndrome
  • Heartburn and acid reflux
  • Dizziness and fatigue
  • Weight changes
  • Appetite changes
  • Sleep issues
  • Higher risk for Type 2 diabetes
  • Anxiety disorders
  • Depressive disorders
  • Weakened immune system

The body attempts to compensate by maintaining the mode (fight, flight, freeze, or fawn). The most effective way to mitigate these stress responses is to activate the parasympathetic nervous system to calm the mind and body.

Soothing the Fight, Flight, or Fawn Response Immediately

Heightened anxiety and panic attacks, the results of an overactive nervous system response, can seem scary and interfere with your daily activities. When stress triggers a response, you need a method or strategies to help ground you in the present and bring your nervous system back into alignment.

The following methods can help soothe these responses. Practice each one several times to see how it works for your situation. The more often you use the strategies, the easier they will be to remember.

5-4-3-2-1 Grounding Technique

The 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique is a simple activity that uses the five senses to keep you in the present and help calm anxious thoughts. With this method, you must concentrate on the items in your environment. You can implement this technique when you feel anxious or at the start of a panic attack.

Take note of your environment. Name five things you see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. Take your time noticing each of the five senses. Note the texture of an item or the aroma.

Deep Breathing

Deep breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system, thereby slowing the heart and respiratory rates. When people become panicked, they tend to breathe more shallowly and faster as they prepare to protect themselves from danger. Unfortunately, this reaction can make you feel dizzy and out of control. Deep breathing regulates these processes.

Try a simple deep breathing exercise. One exercise is the box breathing, which can be done by inhaling deeply through the nose for the count of four. Hold the breath for four to seven beats, and then exhale through the mouth for the count of four to eight.

Another breathing exercise is to inhale deeply through your nose for four seconds, hold for seven seconds, and exhale for eleven seconds. Both exercises can be repeated as necessary. As you inhale, feel your lungs expand to maximize benefit.

Dive Reflex

The dive reflex is elicited by submerging the face in cold water or by splashing cold water on the face, thereby activating the vagus nerve. The vagus nerve is part of the parasympathetic nervous system, also referred to as the rest-and-digest system. This nervous system regulates breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, and digestive function.

To activate the vagus nerve with the dive reflex, submerge your face in cold water for about 30 seconds, ensuring that the skin around your nose and under your eyes is covered. If you would prefer not to submerge your face, you can use a cold pack or a very cold washcloth to cover the areas. Consult a physician before attempting the dive reflex if you have cardiac issues.

Humming a Tune

Have you ever heard someone hum when stressed? Perhaps they were working behind the counter in a busy store or pharmacy, humming while working quickly. Humming activates the vagus nerve through the vibrations coming from the throat. Some people find that humming a tune or singing helps them relax when they are anxious.

When you hum, make sure you can feel the vibration in your throat. You can also make more of a buzzing sound. This vibration “wakes” up the vagus nerve. Most people don’t notice humming, especially when the radio is on or in a hectic crowd, such as while shopping.

Shifting Out of the Freeze Response

Learning to help your nervous system “thaw” and return to alignment after a freeze response will help you get back into your daily routine more quickly. The more you practice these response methods, the faster you will regain control.

Practice is progress. It may not seem that a method is working at first, but consider that even a slight improvement is better than none, and you can build on these small beginnings.

Take Note of Your Environment

During a freeze response, your mind may “zoom” out. You need to “zoom” back into focus by taking note of your environment. Look around and use the 5-4-3-2-1 technique, if possible. Suppose you cannot, try the grounding method on a smaller scale. Reach out and touch one or two items, noting the texture. Name what you hear. Is there a scent you can identify? They now produce small tubes containing essential oils that you can sniff to activate the parasympathetic nervous system.

Make Small Movements to “Thaw”

Sometimes even the smallest movements seem monumental during the freeze response. Try micro-movements initially to help you “thaw.” For example, move your eyes around the room to take in your environment, slowly move one finger at a time, stretching each, or rub a finger against your thumb on the same hand.

Move Your Body When Ready

When you feel you can move your body, use graceful, soft movements rather than hurried reactions. Stand and stretch, move your feet in a shuffle, or do a few marches. Your mind and body are coming back into alignment and need a few minutes to catch up. Don’t try to rush it.

Long-Term Help

The most effective way to treat these responses is to prevent them through lifestyle interventions. Small changes can bring significant results. One new habit could make the next panic attack more manageable. These changes can facilitate emotion regulation, improve physical health, and manage symptoms.

Connect with Others

Anxiety and depressive disorders can keep you from wanting to spend time with others. Many people avoid locations, people, or situations that can trigger panic attacks. However, God did not create you to live in a vacuum. Socialization and connection with others can help shoulder the burden, lift mood, and nurture relationships. Choose a few trusted people to turn to when you feel anxious. Call them or invite them over for coffee or a snack.

Take Exercise Daily

Exercise is a natural anti-anxiety and anti-depressant medication. Engaging in daily exercise will improve physical health while lowering stress hormones and releasing endorphins. These endorphins and other brain chemicals boost mood and regulate emotions. Aim for at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity exercise (thirty minutes on five days per week). When you feel anxious, even a 10-15-minute session could relieve stress and improve your mood.

Seek Professional Help

Professional help is one of the best ways to begin the journey to managing your experience. Seeking help from a medical doctor to ensure there is not anything off or missing physically can assist in maintaining proper responses.

In the same way, seeking help from a mental health practitioner can help you get to the root of your anxiety, manage triggers and symptoms, and learn how to move forward. A counselor will customize a plan for you based on your specific circumstances and assess regularly.

Calming Stress Responses are Possible

You can regulate your body’s stress responses. It takes practice, but you can prevent and manage the freeze response as well as the fight-or-flight response. Contact our office today to consult with a Christian counselor about the best ways to lower your anxiety and worry with counseling and lifestyle interventions.

Photos:

The post How to Soothe the Fight, Flight, Freeze, and Fawn Response  appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: Forgiveness: Bible Verses to Help You Forgive
item.description:
Forgiveness is a topic that sounds easy enough in principle but often feels impossible to put into practice. I remember the grief I felt years ago when the missionary organization I was serving painted me as sexually immoral, sent an email to every religious authority in the small country I was serving in to beware of me, and then let me go with zero proof of actual “sin,” and zero chance for me to defend myself.

This baseless spiritual abuse nearly drove me away from God. It took years before I could forgive my accusers.

We all know the pain of unforgiveness. The one that keeps us awake at night. The one that twists inside us like a knife. How can we extend forgiveness when the person we’re angry with has done the unthinkable? Doesn’t God know what they did to us? How then can He demand we forgive them?

Neuroscience of Resentment

Before we dive into Scripture, I’d like to point out that there are scientific reasons to back up God’s wisdom when it comes to forgiveness. We all know that refusing to forgive an offense can spiral into resentment and bitterness.

As shown in neuro scans studying the effects of unforgiveness, “[r]esentment creates a self-perpetuating cycle (Clark, 2005, as cited in Cherry, n.d.). When you replay what happened, you reactivate the same neural pathways, strengthening the emotional intensity of the memory through long-term potentiation (Kumar, 2011, as cited in Cherry, n.d.).”

This means that the more you ruminate on an event, the more it gets reinforced in your brain’s neural networks, leaving you stuck in the past and secreting cortisol, the stress hormone. Over time, the constant secretion of cortisol and the hyperarousal of the amygdala due to unresolved stress lead to depression, anxiety, and lower self-worth.

“Unforgiveness also correlates with sleep disturbances, cardiovascular problems, elevated blood pressure, weakened immune function, and increased inflammation markers (Abohashem et al., 2024 as cited in Cherry, n.d.; Segerstrom & Miller, 2004 as cited in Cherry, n.d.).”

Rumination leads to cortisol buildup over time. This is due to chronic stress. “Chronic stress causes the muscles in the body to be in a more or less constant state of guardedness. When muscles are taut and tense for long periods of time, this may trigger other reactions of the body and even promote stress-related disorders” (American Psychological Association, 2024).

These stress-related disorders include migraines or chronic headaches because of muscle tension in the neck, shoulders, and head. There are several more systems in the body that get triggered, including the endocrine system, HPA axis, gastrointestinal system, among others (Ibid). Needless to say, unforgiveness is a life stressor that can have far greater consequences than one might expect.

God, creator of the human body, knew this well before the advances of Western medicine. This is why He is so clear in Scripture that forgiveness is essential, not only physically, but spiritually as well. But what exactly does God mean by forgiveness?

What Biblical Forgiveness Is

The purpose of this article is not to use Scripture as a shaming device for those struggling to forgive. There’s a wide misconception about what biblical forgiveness means and what our Western culture makes it out to be. We often think God is asking us to forgive and forget, restore the full trust we had before the offense, or even excuse bad behavior. This is not what the Bible teaches.

If your brother sins against you, go and tell his fault, between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen, take one or two others along with you, that every charge may be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. – Matt. 18:15-17, ESV

Let’s take a closer look at what Jesus is saying in this passage. By using the word “brother,” He’s speaking of a person in the church, i.e., a Christian. Jesus advocates for private reconciliation between Christians wherever possible. He also makes it clear that He’s not speaking of trivial charges, but those of serious merit that can be corroborated by two or three witnesses.

The Greek word used in Matt. 18:15 is a variant of the word hamartánō, which is an archer’s term for missing the mark. A deeper dive into the word explains, “properly, having no share in; to sin, which always brings forfeiture – i.e., eternal loss due to missing God’s mark” (Strong’s Greek: 264).

If this Christian “brother” has refused to reconcile privately despite ample evidence of their wrongdoing, only then should it be brought before a spiritual body. If the offender does not listen to the church and witnesses, they are considered an unbeliever, and thus an outsider to the congregation.

The individual initially seeking reconciliation is also instructed to see them the same way. This denotes removing the closeness and the trust the offender held formerly.

Let’s be clear. Jesus isn’t saying, “Don’t forgive.” By making the offender an outsider of the church, Jesus is providing a way for shame to lead the offender to repentance. Once again, Jesus’ goal is for repentance and forgiveness between Christians, not for Christians to hold grudges or remove fellow believers from the church. Removal from the church is a means to bring the offender to repentance.

Forgiveness is further demonstrated in Matt. 18:21-22, where it says, “Then Peter came up and said to him, ‘Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?’ Jesus said to him, ‘I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven’ (ESV). Jesus asks that we forgive indefinitely. But once again, if the brother doesn’t repent, He’s not asking us to be pushovers.

If we focused solely on these passages, we might think God only asks us to forgive other Christians. But that’s not what’s implied in Matt. 5:44 when Jesus says, “But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (ESV). Paul gives a full description of what it means to love in 1 Corinthians 13.

In 1 Cor. 13:5, love is described as keeping no account of wrongs. The word used is the Greek logizetai. “The term appears in moral contexts where believers weigh motives and actions: 1 Corinthians 13:5: love keeps no account of wrongs;” it does not keep a mental ledger for retaliation (Strong’s Greek: 3049).

So, to love enemies is to keep no account, i.e., no ledger of the wrongs they’ve done against us. The antidote to our vindictiveness toward enemies is given in the same verse in Matt. 5:44, when Jesus tells us to pray for them. By praying for them, we are leaving God room to work on the hearts of our persecutors and replacing bitterness in ourselves with loving, restorative action.

Jesus doesn’t stop with asking us to forgive our brothers (Christians) or enemies (persecutors). He also asks us to love our “neighbor,” which again implies keeping no record of their wrongs. This is evident in Mark 12:31 when Jesus says, “The second [commandment] is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these” (ESV).

Neighbors, as we know from urban living, can be anyone – a Christian, an enemy, a non-Christian, even a complete stranger. Jesus’ command for forgiveness is thus universal. We are to forgive everyone regardless of their believing status.

Two further verses that back this up are Ephesians 4:32: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Ibid), and Colossians 3:13: “[Bear] with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, [forgive] each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive” (ESV).

The Commandment to Forgive

Forgiveness is a command. Notice again in Colossians 3:13 where it states, “as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.” (ESV, emphasis added)

We don’t get a free pass here. Even if we’re angry, even if the offense was great, even if we’re still hurting, we must forgive. Jesus doubles down on this in Matt. 6:14-15 when he says, “For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses (ESV).”

Paul tells us in Romans 12:18-21: If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head.” Do not be overcome by evil but overcome evil with good (ESV).

Conclusion

God doesn’t want us to ruminate. He doesn’t want the chronic stress of unforgiveness to destroy us. He calls us to action. Love our enemies. Pray for them. Do good to them. Feed them. Quench their thirst. Leave God to choose how He wishes to respond to their wrongdoing. There’s so much wisdom in these commands. Psychologically, action is infinitely more healing than inaction.

Forgiveness is a process. We aren’t expected to instantly be okay with what happened to us. With God’s help and our obedience, forgiveness is possible. Even when it feels anything but.

Reference:
American Psychological Association. (2024). Stress Effects on the Body. In American Psychological Association. American Psychological Association. https://www.apa.org/topics/stress/body

Photos:
“Open Bible”, Courtesy of Duncan Kidd, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Hug”, Courtesy of Igor Erico, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Reading the Bible”, Courtesy of Simon Maage, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post Forgiveness: Bible Verses to Help You Forgive appeared first on Spokane Christian Counseling.

If we focused solely on these passages, we might think God only asks us to forgive other Christians. But that’s not what’s implied in Matt. 5:44 when Jesus says, “But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (ESV). Paul gives a full description of what it means to love in 1 Corinthians 13.

In 1 Cor. 13:5, love is described as keeping no account of wrongs. The word used is the Greek logizetai. “The term appears in moral contexts where believers weigh motives and actions: 1 Corinthians 13:5: love keeps no account of wrongs;” it does not keep a mental ledger for retaliation (Strong’s Greek: 3049).

So, to love enemies is to keep no account, i.e., no ledger of the wrongs they’ve done against us. The antidote to our vindictiveness toward enemies is given in the same verse in Matt. 5:44, when Jesus tells us to pray for them. By praying for them, we are leaving God room to work on the hearts of our persecutors and replacing bitterness in ourselves with loving, restorative action.

Jesus doesn’t stop with asking us to forgive our brothers (Christians) or enemies (persecutors). He also asks us to love our “neighbor,” which again implies keeping no record of their wrongs. This is evident in Mark 12:31 when Jesus says, “The second [commandment] is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these” (ESV).

Neighbors, as we know from urban living, can be anyone – a Christian, an enemy, a non-Christian, even a complete stranger. Jesus’ command for forgiveness is thus universal. We are to forgive everyone regardless of their believing status.

Two further verses that back this up are Ephesians 4:32: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Ibid), and Colossians 3:13: “[Bear] with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, [forgive] each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive” (ESV).

The Commandment to Forgive

Forgiveness is a command. Notice again in Colossians 3:13 where it states, “as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.” (ESV, emphasis added)

We don’t get a free pass here. Even if we’re angry, even if the offense was great, even if we’re still hurting, we must forgive. Jesus doubles down on this in Matt. 6:14-15 when he says, “For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses (ESV).”

Paul tells us in Romans 12:18-21: If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head.” Do not be overcome by evil but overcome evil with good (ESV).

Conclusion

God doesn’t want us to ruminate. He doesn’t want the chronic stress of unforgiveness to destroy us. He calls us to action. Love our enemies. Pray for them. Do good to them. Feed them. Quench their thirst. Leave God to choose how He wishes to respond to their wrongdoing. There’s so much wisdom in these commands. Psychologically, action is infinitely more healing than inaction.

Forgiveness is a process. We aren’t expected to instantly be okay with what happened to us. With God’s help and our obedience, forgiveness is possible. Even when it feels anything but.

item.title: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) for Treating Major Depressive Disorders
item.description:
All human beings experience negative or sad moods at times. However, if these or other symptoms are making it hard to function, you may be suffering from clinical depression. A clinical diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) requires five or more symptoms over the same two-week period, including either a depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure, plus significant distress, or impaired functioning.

Although not a complete list, symptoms may include agitation, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, problems with thinking, concentrating, or making decisions, recurring thoughts of death, suicidal thoughts, or suicide attempts.

These symptoms are a change from prior functioning and are not due to another medical condition or substance use. Whether or not you meet the full clinical criteria, seeking out therapy is appropriate if you are experiencing symptoms that distress you or limit your full engagement in life.

Medication for Major Depressive Disorders

Antidepressant medications have been a profoundly helpful tool for managing or recovering from Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). Yet some patients prefer tapering off medications after symptoms decrease, due to unwanted side effects, expense, or other concerns. Other individuals have not experienced a substantial response even after trials of several different medications or prefer non-pharmacological approaches for other reasons.

Because some patients do not respond optimally to the first antidepressant, adding or switching to a different type of antidepressant is also a common scenario. Per the National Institute of Mental Health, even when some symptoms start to improve quickly, full therapeutic effects may take 4-8 weeks for many individuals.

Thankfully, medications are not the only effective depression treatment. Many MDD studies have reported that combining psychotherapy with antidepressant medication yields better outcomes than medication alone, especially for moderate to severe depression. Psychotherapy can help with initial symptom remission, maintaining progress, treatment satisfaction, and preventing relapses.

Therefore, evidence-based psychotherapies can be a powerful ally for recovery from depression, even for those already on medication. Research also indicates that the quality of the working relationship is more important to depression treatment outcomes than theoretical orientation by itself. It is vitally important to find a therapist with whom you are comfortable and can build a strong, trusting rapport.

Cognitive Behavioral therapies for depression have been particularly well studied. Generally speaking, these therapy approaches consider the impact of thinking and behaviors upon mood. Original Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) emphasized that automatic errors in thinking, such as catastrophizing or predominantly focusing on the negative aspects of situations, contribute to depressed mood.

CBT suggested that depressed individuals have disproportionately negative views of themselves, others, and their futures. Learning to correct thinking errors while also increasing constructive, rewarding behaviors are central components of CBT work. Well-implemented CBT has held up over decades as an effective depression treatment, albeit not the only one.

Today, many clinicians employ newer-generation cognitive behavioral therapies, which still consider depressive thought patterns. Instead of correcting faulty thoughts, however, the client’s focus is on changing their relationship to these thoughts.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy

For example, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) helps clients reduce attachment to unhelpful thinking by learning to observe thoughts as passing mental events rather than facts. Clients also work on acceptance of internal experiences and feelings. Acceptance does not mean that one must like all thoughts and emotions – only that their existence is observed and acknowledged.

Importantly, the next step is to take committed actions that are consistent with personal values, regardless of the current thoughts, internal sensations, and feelings. Rather than battling negative internal thoughts, the thoughts are noted, but energy is consciously redirected toward pursuing personally meaningful goals.

More specifically, six core processes are addressed by the therapist during the process of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy.

Work revolves around accepting the full range of thoughts and emotions, identifying and distancing from transient thoughts and emotions, increasing mindful awareness of the present moment, understanding one’s broader life context and the roles and meaning within it, identifying personal values, and taking committed action toward personally valued goals.

Throughout the process, clients are encouraged to observe patterns and track thoughts and behaviors that move them toward or away from desired goals. In this way, clients learn to improve psychological flexibility, giving them a healthier range of responses to life events and difficult emotions.

If you are struggling with symptoms of depression and these principles appeal to you, I encourage you to seek out a therapist trained in ACT. A skilled clinician can partner with you, using this evidence-based approach to treating depression and other mood disorders.

References:
American Psychiatric Association. (2022). Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed.). https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.books.9780890425787
Rush, A. J., Trivedi, M. H., Wisniewski, S. R., Stewart, J. W., Nierenberg, A. A., Thase, M. E., Ritz, L., Biggs, M. M., Warden, D., Luther, J. F., Shores-Wilson, K., Niederehe, G., & Fava, M. (2006). “Bupropion-SR, sertraline, or venlafaxine-XR after failure of SSRIs for depression.”, New England Journal of Medicine, 354(12), 1231–1242. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa052963.
Trivedi, M. H., Fava, M., Wisniewski, S. R., Thase, M. E., Quitkin, F., Warden, D., Ritz, L., Nierenberg, A. A., Lebowitz, B. D., Biggs, M. M., Luther, J. F., Shores-Wilson, K., & Rush, A. J. (2006). “Medication augmentation after the failure of SSRIs for depression.”, New England Journal of Medicine, 354(12), 1243–1252. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa052964.
Cuijpers, P., Noma, H., Karyotaki, E., Vinkers, C. H., Cipriani, A., & Furukawa, T. A. (2020). “A network meta‐analysis of the effects of psychotherapies, pharmacotherapies and their combination in the treatment of adult depression.”, World Psychiatry, 19(1), 92-107.
Wampold, B. E. (2015). “How important are the common factors in psychotherapy? An update.”, World Psychiatry, 14, 270–277.
Beck, A. T., & Haigh, E. A. P. (2014). “Advances in cognitive theory and therapy: The generic cognitive model.”, Annual Review of Clinical Psychology, 10, 1–24.
Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (2012). Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: The Process and Practice of Mindful Change (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.
